address_cn: 四川省成都市青羊区青华路37号
hook: The thatched hut where China's greatest poet wrote 240 masterpieces during four years of exile — now a 300-acre garden museum where red walls, bamboo groves, and plum blossoms create the exact atmosphere of the poems themselves.
honest_description: Du Fu Thatched Cottage is part literary shrine, part classical Chinese garden, and part peaceful urban escape. The site commemorates Tang Dynasty poet Du Fu (712-770), who fled to Chengdu during a rebellion and spent four years in a modest hut writing some of China's most celebrated poems. The actual cottage is a reconstruction, but the surrounding garden is genuinely beautiful — red-walled walkways shaded by bamboo, lotus ponds, plum blossom groves, and traditional Sichuan architecture. The museum section houses extensive collections of Du Fu's poetry, calligraphy, and historical artifacts, including a newly added modern museum with AR/VR experiences. If you appreciate Chinese poetry and literature, this is sacred ground. If you don't know Du Fu, you can still enjoy it as a gorgeous garden — but hiring a guide or using the audio tour transforms the experience from 'pretty park' to 'deeply meaningful.' The red-walled bamboo corridor has become a social media sensation, especially for hanfu (traditional costume) photography.

foreigner_top_questions.question: Is it worth visiting if I don't know Chinese poetry?
foreigner_top_questions.answer: Yes, but with a caveat. The gardens alone are beautiful enough to justify the visit — the red-walled bamboo pathways, lotus ponds, and traditional architecture make for a peaceful 2-3 hour stroll. However, without context about Du Fu, you'll miss the emotional resonance that makes this site meaningful to Chinese visitors. Hiring an English-speaking guide or using the audio tour (available via the official WeChat account) dramatically improves the experience. Du Fu is essentially the Shakespeare of Chinese poetry — understanding even a few of his poems transforms the visit. If you'd like a quick primer before visiting, message our team and we can send you a short English guide to Du Fu's key poems and their connection to the cottage — or arrange an English-speaking guide to bring the poetry to life on-site.

foreigner_top_questions.question: How do I get tickets as a foreigner?
foreigner_top_questions.answer: Buy at the gate ticket window with your passport for ¥50 (or ¥47 online through Ctrip/Trip.com). Unlike many Beijing attractions, advance booking is not mandatory — you can walk up and buy. Note: the free admission for Chinese seniors (60+) does NOT apply to foreign passport holders. Bring your physical passport or a clear photo of it.

experience_format_note: Self-guided museum and garden visit. The main buildings are arranged along a central axis: Main Gate → Dagai Hall → Poetry History Hall → Chai Gate → Gongbu Shrine. The garden surrounds this axis with multiple paths to explore. No structured route — wander freely. Audio guides available via the official WeChat account 'Du Fu Thatched Cottage Museum' (free, Chinese and English).
vibe: A poet's garden that feels exactly as it should — hushed, green, thoughtful, and just melancholy enough to make you sit on a stone bench and think about life.

time_needed.quick_visit: 1.5-2 hours (central axis buildings and the main garden)
time_needed.recommended: 3-4 hours (full exploration including museum, garden, archaeological site, and tea in the bamboo grove)
time_needed.deep_dive: Half day (everything above plus the modern museum with AR experiences, the calligraphy exhibitions, and lingering in the garden)

best_time.best_time_of_day: Late afternoon (3-5 PM) when tour groups thin out and soft light filters through the bamboo. Early morning (9-10 AM) is also peaceful.
best_time.worst_time: Chinese public holidays and weekends, especially spring when the plum blossoms draw extra crowds. The red-wall bamboo corridor gets extremely congested with hanfu photographers on weekends.
best_time.seasonal_notes: Spring (March-May): plum blossoms, cherry blossoms, and fresh bamboo shoots — the garden is at its most photogenic. Summer: lush greenery and lotus flowers in the ponds, but hot and humid. Autumn: golden ginkgo leaves. Winter: bare but atmospheric, with the occasional snow on the thatched cottage roofs.
best_time.pro_tip: Visit on a weekday afternoon in late autumn — the garden is peaceful, ginkgo leaves are golden, and you can enjoy the outdoor tea garden in comfortable weather.

getting_in.price_rmb: ¥50/person (full price); ¥25 (student); free for Chinese citizens 60+ (foreigners pay full price)

Worth it if staying in Chengdu for an extended period

getting_in.booking_required: No — walk-up purchase available. Online booking optional (slightly cheaper). During peak holidays, capacity limits may apply — booking ahead is safer.
getting_in.booking_method: Buy at the gate with passport, or online via Ctrip/Trip.com/official WeChat account. Present QR code or passport at entrance.
getting_in.passport_accepted: Yes — present passport at ticket window. A photo of your passport may also be accepted.
getting_in.what_to_bring: Passport or passport photo. Camera. Comfortable walking shoes. The garden has many photo opportunities — consider traditional costume rental shops nearby if interested in hanfu photography.
getting_in.queue_situation: Minimal queuing on weekdays — under 5 minutes. Weekends and holidays may see 15-30 minute waits at the ticket window. Inside, the red-wall corridor can be congested with photographers.
getting_in.language_barrier_rating: some-chinese-helps — Major buildings have bilingual signage (Chinese/English). Poetry displays are mostly in Chinese only. The audio guide (via WeChat) offers English. Guides in English can be arranged through tour platforms.

highlights.name: Poetry History Hall (诗史堂)
highlights.description: The central hall displaying Du Fu's life story and his 1,400+ poems categorized as 'poetry history' — poetic records of the tumultuous Tang Dynasty. Houses sculptures and calligraphy.
highlights.foreigner_note: Du Fu is called the 'Poet Sage' (诗圣) — his poetry documented war, famine, and social injustice during the An Lushan Rebellion. He's the Chinese equivalent of Shakespeare or Homer in cultural importance.
highlights.tip: Use the audio guide here — the historical context transforms what looks like a plain hall into an emotional experience. The calligraphy on the walls is by famous artists across centuries.

highlights.name: The Thatched Cottage (茅屋)
highlights.description: A reconstructed straw-roofed hut recreating Du Fu's modest dwelling, surrounded by a stream, garden, and bamboo. This is where he wrote his most famous poem 'Song of My Thatched Roof Torn by Autumn Winds.'
highlights.foreigner_note: The poem written here — about his roof being torn off in a storm — ends with the line '安得广厦千万间' (If only there were millions of mansions to shelter all the cold scholars). It became one of the most quoted lines in Chinese literature.
highlights.tip: Stand by the stream and listen to the water and birdsong — the atmosphere deliberately recreates the scenes Du Fu described in his poetry.

highlights.name: Red-Wall Bamboo Corridor (红墙竹影)
highlights.description: A photogenic walkway flanked by crimson walls with overhanging bamboo creating dappled shadows — the most photographed spot in the entire complex and a social media sensation.
highlights.foreigner_note: This has become Chengdu's most Instagrammed spot. You'll see many Chinese visitors in hanfu (traditional costume) posing here — it's a beautiful scene even to photograph the photographers.
highlights.tip: Come early morning or late afternoon for the best light filtering through bamboo. On weekdays, you can get a crowd-free shot. On weekends, expect to queue for your turn.

highlights.name: Archaeological Site (唐代遗址)
highlights.description: An actual Tang Dynasty archaeological excavation site within the complex, believed to be near Du Fu's original dwelling. Covered with a modern protective structure displaying the layers of 1,300-year-old foundations.
highlights.foreigner_note: This is rare tangible evidence connecting the literary tradition to a physical place — most ancient Chinese literary sites are purely commemorative.
highlights.tip: Easy to miss as it's in the eastern section of the complex. Look for the modern building covering the excavation pit.

what_visitors_miss.what: The outdoor tea garden in the bamboo grove
what_visitors_miss.why: Multiple tea gardens within the complex offer traditional Chengdu gaiwan tea service under bamboo canopy — the perfect way to absorb the garden's atmosphere. A bowl of tea is ¥15-30 and comes with snacks.

what_visitors_miss.what: The creative souvenirs and calligraphy shop
what_visitors_miss.why: The gift shop actually has high-quality merchandise — traditional calligraphy sets, poetry-themed designs, and artisanal items that are genuinely worth buying. Staff are passionate and knowledgeable.

what_visitors_miss.what: The modern museum with AR/VR experiences
what_visitors_miss.why: A recently added section with digital exhibitions using AR glasses, AI interactions with a digital 'Du Fu,' and immersive poetry experiences. Combines technology with tradition in a surprisingly effective way.

strategy.smart_route: Enter through the main gate → follow the central axis (Dagai Hall → Poetry History Hall → Chai Gate → Gongbu Shrine) for the historical narrative → detour west to the Thatched Cottage and plum garden → walk the red-wall bamboo corridor → visit the archaeological site in the east section → end at the modern museum → have tea in the bamboo grove tea garden before leaving.
strategy.what_to_skip: Skip the main gate souvenir stalls (the inside gift shop is much better). If time is limited, the western garden paths between the cottage and the plum garden are the most scenic but least essential for understanding Du Fu.
strategy.pro_tips: Rent an audio guide or follow the official WeChat audio tour — it transforms the experience completely. If visiting with children, the modern museum's interactive AR exhibits make the poetry engaging even for kids. The calligraphy shop near the exit sells 'Fallen Plum Blossom Cards' (拾梅笺) — free cards you can use to collect fallen blossoms from the garden.

heads_up.warning: Without context, it can feel like 'just a park'
heads_up.advice: Du Fu's significance isn't obvious to non-Chinese speakers. Invest in a guide or audio tour — it's the difference between a pleasant garden walk and a deeply meaningful cultural experience.

heads_up.warning: The red-wall corridor is a photography circus on weekends
heads_up.advice: Professional photographers and hanfu-wearing visitors can dominate the corridor for extended periods. Visit on a weekday or arrive right at opening to get your shot. If you're interested in doing a hanfu photoshoot yourself, message our team — we can recommend the best rental shops near the cottage and help you book a time slot.

heads_up.warning: Getting a taxi/Didi after visiting can be difficult
heads_up.advice: The area around the museum is congested and ride-hailing pickup points are limited. Walk a few blocks out before calling a car, or take metro Line 4 (Caotang Beilu Station, ~20 min walk). If you're having trouble getting a ride after your visit, message us and we can arrange a car to pick you up from a nearby meeting point.

foreigners_watch_out: Foreign passport holders must pay ¥50 even if over 60 — the free senior admission only applies to Chinese ID holders.
Poetry displays and most exhibit text are in Chinese only — the English signage covers building descriptions but not the actual poetry content. The audio guide fills this gap.
The WeChat audio guide is free but requires the WeChat app — download and set up before your visit.
Metro Line 13 to Du Fu Thatched Cottage Station (Exit C2) is the closest metro, about a 400m walk. Buses 35, 58, 82 also reach the area.

if_things_go_wrong.problem: Arrived without cash or working digital payment
if_things_go_wrong.what_to_do: The ticket office accepts WeChat Pay, Alipay, and cash. If none work, try buying via Ctrip/Trip.com app (accepts foreign cards).
if_things_go_wrong.plan_b: The adjacent Huanhuaxi Park (浣花溪公园) is free and connects to the same green space — you can enjoy the riverside walk without entering the paid area.

if_things_go_wrong.what_to_do: Head to the eastern and northern sections of the garden — the western axis and red-wall corridor draw most visitors. The archaeological site area and modern museum are typically less crowded.
if_things_go_wrong.plan_b: The outdoor tea gardens are always relaxing even when the paths are busy — sit down, order tea, and wait for crowds to thin in the late afternoon.

preparation.what_to_wear: Comfortable walking shoes. The garden paths are well-maintained but extensive. Light layers — Chengdu can be cool even in spring/autumn.
preparation.what_to_bring: Passport. Camera. Phone with WeChat installed (for audio guide). Cash or mobile payment. Umbrella (Chengdu is frequently drizzly).
preparation.what_not_to_bring: Nothing to avoid specifically. Tripods are allowed but may cause congestion in the red-wall corridor.

physical_accessibility.physical_details: Almost entirely flat terrain across 300 acres of gardens. Paved paths throughout. Wheelchair accessible on main routes. Total walking distance for a full visit is about 3-4km but at a leisurely pace.
physical_accessibility.age_notes: Suitable for all ages. Stroller-friendly on main paths. Benches and tea houses provide ample rest opportunities. Children may find the modern museum's AR experiences engaging.
physical_accessibility.health_warnings: No significant health risks. Chengdu humidity can be tiring in summer. Mosquitoes are present near the ponds — insect repellent helps in summer.

concierge_opportunities.action: Book an English-speaking guide for the museum
concierge_opportunities.platform: Klook, Trip.com, or arrange through hotel concierge
concierge_opportunities.value_to_user: Transforms the visit from a garden stroll into a deep cultural experience. Guides explain the poetry, history, and significance in ways that English signage cannot. We can match you with a guide who specializes in Chinese literature and history — someone who can recite the poems and explain why they still matter 1,200 years later.

pair_with.why: A free riverside park adjacent to the cottage complex — extends the garden experience along the Flower Washing Stream that Du Fu wrote about.

pair_with.suggestion: Wuhou Temple / Jinli Street (武侯祠/锦里)
pair_with.why: Chengdu's other major historical site (Three Kingdoms era) paired with its most famous commercial ancient street. Together with Du Fu's Cottage, covers Chengdu's top cultural attractions.

pair_with.suggestion: Wide and Narrow Alleys (宽窄巷子)
pair_with.why: Chengdu's renovated Qing Dynasty alley district with tea houses, restaurants, and cultural performances — a more lively counterpoint to the serene cottage.

cultural_context: Du Fu (712-770) is universally regarded as China's greatest realist poet, earning the title 'Poet Sage' (诗圣). During the devastating An Lushan Rebellion (755-763), he fled to Chengdu and spent four years in a simple thatched hut by the Flower Washing Stream, writing over 240 poems that documented the suffering of ordinary people during wartime. His most famous poem from this period, 'Song of My Thatched Roof Torn by Autumn Winds,' ends with the selfless wish: 'If only I could get a mansion of millions of rooms, to shelter all the world's cold and poor scholars!' This sentiment — a poet in poverty caring more about others' suffering than his own — became a foundational ideal in Chinese culture. The cottage has been commemorated and rebuilt multiple times over 1,200 years, with the current layout dating to the Ming-Qing period.

photo_spots.tip: Early morning (9-10 AM) or golden hour light through bamboo creates the most dramatic shadows on the red walls. Weekday mornings for empty corridor shots.
photo_spots.why: Chengdu's most photographed spot — the contrast of crimson walls, green bamboo, and dappled shadow is irresistible.

photo_spots.tip: Step back to include the stream, bamboo, and cottage roof in one frame. Spring plum blossoms add color in March.
photo_spots.why: The reconstructed cottage surrounded by nature captures the essence of Du Fu's poetry — simplicity within beauty.

photo_spots.tip: Visit in July-August when lotus flowers are in full bloom. The reflection shots with traditional architecture are stunning.
photo_spots.why: Classical Chinese garden photography at its finest — lotus, stone bridge, and curved rooflines.

card_hook: Where China's greatest poet turned suffering into immortal verse.
